The Philosophy

From linear waste
to circular value.

The traditional economy runs in a straight line — resources extracted, products consumed, waste discarded. Seebury's circular economy model closes every loop: materials re-enter manufacturing, organic waste becomes energy, and contaminated streams become clean outputs.

Design for the next cycle,
not the landfill.

Every ton of municipal solid waste that enters a Seebury facility exits as something valuable — vehicle-ready diesel, biochar for graphene production, electricity for the grid, compost for agriculture, or clean glass fiber for the next generation of manufacturing.

The Seebury circular economy platform spans six service verticals — solar, wind, natural gas, waste-to-energy, green hydrogen, and recycling — each feeding into the others to maximize value from every material and energy stream.

The Seebury Circular Loop
Collect
Municipal solid waste, food waste, yard waste collected and transported to the Seebury Materials Recovery Facility (MRF)
Sort & Recover
Hyper MRF sorts recyclables (glass, metal, paper, plastic) using laser sorting. Organic material separated for anaerobic digestion or pyrolysis feedstock conditioning.
Convert
Pyrolysis converts carbon-rich material to syngas → diesel and biochar. SMARTFERM AD converts organics to biogas (→ CNG) and compost.
Generate
Waste-to-Energy plant converts Refuse Derived Fuel (RDF) to electricity and thermal energy for the grid and on-site operations.
Return
Recyclables return to manufacturing. Compost to agriculture. Diesel to fuel market. Biochar to graphene production. Zero to landfill.
Waste-to-Energy

The Seebury pyrolysis platform converts municipal solid waste into three simultaneous revenue streams — vehicle-ready diesel fuel, pipeline-quality gas, and grid electricity — with zero emissions and zero landfill. Proven technology used commercially since the 1800s, now scaled to 1,000 tons per day.

Seebury Eco Campus

The complete
recycling center model.

The Seebury Eco Campus integrates a Materials Recovery Facility, anaerobic digestion (SMARTFERM AD), and a Waste-to-Energy plant under one campus — processing every waste stream into a saleable output. Municipal solid waste, food waste, and yard waste each follow their optimal pathway to maximum value recovery.

The campus is designed around the principle that no material should have only one pathway. MSW enters the Materials Recovery Facility and is immediately sorted — recyclables stream to manufacturing markets, carbon-rich material goes to the pyrolysis plant, and organic material feeds the SMARTFERM Anaerobic Digester.

The SMARTFERM AD system converts food waste and yard waste into biogas (upgraded to CNG for vehicle fuel), plus high-quality compost for agricultural markets. The WTE plant processes Refuse Derived Fuel into electricity and heat.

🚛

MSW Collection → Materials Recovery Facility

Laser sorting separates recyclables (glass, metal, paper, plastic) from RDF and organic feedstock

🍃

Anaerobic digestion produces biogas → CNG vehicle fuel + compost for agriculture

⚡

RDF → Waste-to-Energy Plant

Refuse Derived Fuel converted to electricity and thermal energy for grid and campus

🔄

All Streams → Zero Landfill

Every input exits as fuel, electricity, biogas, compost, or recyclable material. Nothing buried.

PFAS — Forever Chemicals

Breaking the PFAS cycle.

PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) — known as "forever chemicals" — cycle from industrial sources through landfills, wastewater treatment, farmland, and drinking water in a persistent contamination loop. Seebury's advanced waste treatment platform intercepts this cycle before it reaches groundwater and communities.

PFAS enter the environment from industrial manufacturing, firefighting foam, and treated food packaging. They migrate through landfill leachate to wastewater treatment plants, where conventional treatment fails to eliminate them. The result: PFAS in biosolids spread on farmland, infiltrating groundwater, and ultimately reaching residential drinking water supplies.

How the PFAS cycle compounds:

PFAS-producing industries discharge wastewater to treatment plants. Landfills generate PFAS leachate. Biosolids from treatment are spread on soil. Firefighting foam deposits PFAS directly in groundwater. Every pathway eventually reaches the same destination: residential drinking water.

The Seebury intervention:

Advanced pyrolysis treatment destroys PFAS compounds at the temperatures reached during the pyrolysis process — breaking the "forever chemical" bond that makes conventional treatment ineffective. By processing contaminated waste streams through the Seebury pyrolysis platform, PFAS-bearing materials are destroyed rather than redistributed.

Seebury Solution

High-temperature pyrolysis destroys PFAS compounds that survive conventional wastewater treatment. Contaminated biosolids, industrial waste, and PFAS-bearing materials are processed through the closed-loop system — eliminating the contamination pathway rather than relocating it. The output is clean fuel, clean fiber, and clean electricity — not PFAS-laden biosolids applied to farmland.

Source: Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy (EGLE) — Official PFAS Cycle Diagram
PFAS contamination pathways from industrial sources through landfill, wastewater, farmland, and drinking water
